module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Cuban Primes

OEIS A002407 lists the primes that are differences of two consecutive positive cubes. The
sequence is conjectured to be infinite.

*References:*
- [OEIS A002407](https://oeis.org/A002407)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace OeisA2407

/-- A natural number is in A002407 when it is prime and is the difference of two consecutive
positive cubes. The addition equality avoids truncated subtraction in `ℕ`. -/
def A (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p.Prime ∧ ∃ k > 0, p + k ^ 3 = (k + 1) ^ 3

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_7 : A 7 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 1, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_19 : A 19 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 2, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_37 : A 37 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 3, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_61 : A 61 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 4, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_127 : A 127 := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, 6, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_a_91 : ¬ A 91 := by
  norm_num [A, Nat.prime_def_lt]

/--
This sequence is believed to be infinite.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem conjecture : {p : ℕ | A p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end OeisA2407

reformulations.difference: The Lean membership predicate is `p.Prime ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, k > 0 ∧ p + k ^ 3 = (k + 1) ^ 3`: it is restricted to positive natural k ("consecutive positive cubes" in the docstring) and phrased additively. The OEIS name says "primes which are the difference of two consecutive cubes", with no sign restriction, and a comment gives "Equivalently, primes of the form p = 1+3k(k+1)".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: In ℕ the additive equation is exactly p = (k+1)^3 − k^3 = 3k²+3k+1, with no truncated subtraction. Over ℤ, (y+1)^3 − y^3 = 3y²+3y+1 is invariant under y ↦ −1−y, so negative y give the same values as nonnegative y. y ∈ {0, −1} gives 1, which is not prime, so requiring k > 0 excludes no prime. Proved in Lean (no sorry): `A p ↔ p.Prime ∧ ∃ x y : ℤ, x = y + 1 ∧ (p : ℤ) = x ^ 3 - y ^ 3` and `A p ↔ p.Prime ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, p = 1 + 3 * k * (k + 1)`. As a sanity check, the members below 30000 are exactly the first 42 terms of the OEIS b-file.

sources_consulted: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A002/A002407.seq (official OEIS data repository; full A002407 entry, revision #214, Jun 28 2026 — oeis.org's HTML page was behind a Cloudflare challenge)

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13641 and its LaTeX e-print (M. Wills 2025, linked from the OEIS entry; remark: "These are the Cuban primes ... A002407 in the OEIS. This sequence is conjectured to be infinite.")
review.notes: I checked every declaration. `A` elaborates entirely in ℕ (confirmed with `#print`). The five `a_*` tests (k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6) and `not_a_91` (91 = 6^3 − 5^3 = 7·13) are correct. `conjecture` is `{p | A p}.Infinite`, which is the OEIS comment "This sequence is believed to be infinite" (Sloane, May 2020), quoted verbatim in the docstring. It is written as a plain statement, as CONTRIBUTING prefers for non-question conjectures. `research open` is the correct status. The claim is the Bunyakovsky/Bateman–Horn conjecture for the irreducible polynomial 3k²+3k+1, and no polynomial of degree ≥ 2 is known to take infinitely many prime values. A 2025 paper cited by the entry still calls it conjectural. The module docstring's "positive cubes" differs from OEIS's unqualified "consecutive cubes", but the two are provably equivalent (see reformulations), and Wikipedia's definition also takes y > 0.
